title: Building a Walnut Bench With Only Hand Tools
creator: Ben Calloway
description:
A walnut entry bench, no power tools, three weekends. Through-tenons, a bit of drawboring, and one dovetail I'm not proud of.

Plans for this bench (PDF, cut list, full-size templates): callowayworkshop.com/plans
Shop aprons and the occasional t-shirt: callowayworkshop.com/shop

sentences.t: This slab of walnut has been leaning against my shop wall for two years, and today it finally becomes a bench.
No power tools on this one, just saws, planes, chisels and a lot of coffee.
It's going by our front door, so it needs to hold two kids pulling boots on and off, every morning, forever.
First job is breaking it down, and with a rip saw that is a workout, I'm not going to lie.
Long, even strokes, let the saw do the work, which is what everyone says and nobody actually does.
I'm cutting about a sixteenth outside the line, because the plane is going to take me the rest of the way.
Twenty minutes for one cut, and my shoulder is already filing a complaint.
Then flattening, and this is where the jack plane earns its keep, diagonal strokes across the grain first.
Okay, quick thing while I catch my breath, because people ask me about this every single video.
The plans for this bench are on my website, callowayworkshop dot com, it's a PDF with the cut list and full size templates for the legs.
It's twelve dollars, and it's honestly how I keep this channel going without having to put a sponsor in every video.
There are also shop aprons up there, the same waxed canvas one I'm wearing, my wife sews every one of them in the back room.
If you've bought anything from the shop, thank you, it really does pay for the walnut.
Alright, legs.
I'm laying out through-tenons, which means the tenon goes all the way through the seat and you see the end grain on top.
Marking gauge set to a third of the leg thickness, scribe both cheeks, then saw down the waste side of the line.
Slow down on the last half inch, that's where you blow out the shoulder if you rush it.
Then the mortise in the seat, and this is the scary part, because a mistake here ruins the whole slab.
Drill out most of the waste with a brace and bit, then pare to the line with a wide chisel.
Check for square constantly, every few cuts, I'm holding a little square right up against the chisel.
Okay, test fit, and, it's tight, which is good, tight is good.
Now I'm going to drawbore these, which is an old trick where you offset the peg hole by a hair.
When you drive the peg in, it pulls the joint tighter, so it'll hold even if the glue fails someday.
I'm using oak pegs, riven, not sawn, because riven pegs follow the grain and they don't snap.
Tap, tap, and listen, the sound changes when it's fully seated, it goes from a thud to a ring.
Last, the stretcher, and this is where my one bad dovetail lives, which I'll show you, because honesty.
See that gap, that's where I sawed on the wrong side of the line, I filled it with a walnut shaving and some glue.
Nobody will ever notice except me, and now all of you.
Finish is just boiled linseed oil, three coats, a day apart, and then a coat of paste wax.
Look at that grain come up, this is the moment that makes the whole three weekends worth it.
Kids have already sat on it, nobody's fallen through, so I'm calling that a success.
Thanks for watching, and I'll see you next time in the shop.
